paragraphs: Many ingenious arguments have been put forward to account for and excuse the tyranny of man, arguments meant to prove that in acquiring virtue the two sexes ought to aim at quite different characters. To put it plainly, women are not granted enough strength of mind to acquire anything that truly deserves the name of virtue. Yet, if we allow that they have souls, it would seem that providence has appointed only one way to lead MANKIND to either virtue or happiness.

If, then, women are not a swarm of triflers who live, like mayflies, for a single day, why should they be kept ignorant under the plausible name of innocence? Men complain, and rightly, of the follies and whims of our sex, when they are not busy savagely satirizing our headstrong passions and grovelling vices. Look, I would answer, at the natural effect of ignorance! A mind with nothing but prejudices to rest on will always be unstable, and a current will rush on with destructive fury when there are no barriers to break its force. From infancy women are told, and taught by their mothers’ example, that a little knowledge of human weakness (rightly called cunning), a soft temper, OUTWARD obedience and a scrupulous attention to a childish sort of propriety will win them the protection of man; and that if they are beautiful, nothing else is needed, for at least twenty years of their lives.

That is how Milton describes our first frail mother. Yet when he tells us that women are formed for softness and sweet attractive grace, I cannot understand what he means, unless, in the true Mahometan manner, he meant to deny us souls and to hint that we were beings designed, by sweet attractive grace and docile blind obedience, solely to gratify the senses of man when he can no longer soar on the wing of contemplation.

How grossly they insult us who advise us in this way to make ourselves nothing more than gentle domestic animals! Consider, for example, that winning softness, so warmly and so often recommended, which governs by obeying. What childish language! And how insignificant is the being — can it be an immortal one? — who will stoop to govern by such underhand methods! “Certainly,” says Lord Bacon, “man is of kin to the beasts by his body: and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit, he is a base and ignoble creature!” Men, it seems to me, act in a thoroughly unphilosophical way when they try to secure the good conduct of women by trying to keep them forever in a state of childhood. Rousseau was more consistent when he wished to halt the progress of reason in both sexes; for if men eat of the tree of knowledge, women will come in for a taste. But since their understandings now receive only an imperfect cultivation, all they acquire is a knowledge of evil.

Children, I grant, should be innocent; but applied to men or women, the word is merely a polite name for weakness. For if we allow that Providence destined women to acquire human virtues, and, by exercising their understandings, to gain that stability of character which is the firmest ground for our hopes of the future, then they must be permitted to turn to the fountain of light itself, and not be forced to steer by the twinkling of a mere satellite. Milton, I grant, thought very differently, for he bows only to the indefeasible right of beauty; though it would be hard to reconcile the two passages I now intend to set side by side. But great men are often led by their senses into inconsistencies of this kind: —

“To whom thus Eve with perfect beauty adorned: My author and disposer, what thou bidst Unargued I obey; so God ordains; God is thy law, thou mine; to know no more Is woman’s happiest knowledge and her praise.”

These are precisely the arguments I have used with children, except that I have added: “Your reason is growing stronger now, and until it reaches some degree of maturity you must look up to me for advice; after that you ought to THINK, and to rely on God alone.”
Yet in the following lines Milton seems to agree with me, when he has Adam remonstrate with his Maker in these words: —

“Hast thou not made me here thy substitute, And these inferior far beneath me set? Among unequals what society Can sort, what harmony or delight? Which must be mutual, in proportion due Given and received; but in disparity The one intense, the other still remiss Cannot well suit with either, but soon prove Tedious alike: of fellowship I speak Such as I seek fit to participate All rational delight.”

In discussing the conduct and character of women, therefore, let us set sensual arguments aside and work out what we should try to make of them, so that they may co-operate, if the expression is not too bold, with the Supreme Being.

By individual education I mean — for the sense of the term has not been precisely fixed — the kind of attention to a child that will gradually sharpen the senses, shape the temper, regulate the passions as they begin to stir, and set the understanding to work before the body is mature; so that the grown man need only continue the important task of learning to think and reason, not begin it.

To prevent any misreading, I must add that I do not believe a private education can work the wonders that some over-hopeful writers have credited it with. Men and women must be educated, to a great extent, by the opinions and customs of the society they live in. In every age a current of popular opinion has swept all before it and given the century, as it were, a family likeness. We may fairly infer, then, that until society is differently constituted, not much can be expected from education. For my present purpose, however, it is enough to assert that, whatever effect circumstances have on the abilities, every being can become virtuous by exercising its own reason. For if even one being were created with vicious inclinations — that is, positively bad — what could save us from atheism? Or, if we worship a God, would that God not be a devil?

It follows that the most perfect education, in my view, is the kind of exercise of the understanding best suited to strengthen the body and form the heart — or, in other words, to enable the individual to acquire such habits of virtue as will make it independent. Indeed, it is a farce to call any being virtuous whose virtues do not spring from the exercise of its own reason. Rousseau held this opinion about men; I extend it to women, and I confidently assert that they have been drawn out of their proper sphere by false refinement, not by any effort to acquire masculine qualities. Still, the royal homage they receive is so intoxicating that, until the morals and customs of the age change and come to rest on more reasonable principles, it may be impossible to convince them of two things: that the illegitimate power they gain by degrading themselves is a curse, and that they must return to nature and equality if they wish to secure the calm contentment that natural, unspoiled affections bring. But for that era we must wait — wait, perhaps, until kings and nobles, enlightened by reason and preferring the real dignity of man to childish pomp, throw off their gaudy inherited trappings; and if even then women do not give up the arbitrary power of beauty, they will prove that they have LESS mind than man. I may be accused of arrogance, yet I must declare what I firmly believe: every writer on female education and manners, from Rousseau to Dr. Gregory, has helped to make women more artificial and weaker in character than they would otherwise have been, and consequently more useless members of society. I could have stated this conviction in a gentler tone; but I fear that would have been the whine of affectation, not a faithful expression of my feelings and of the clear conclusion that experience and reflection have led me to draw. When I come to that part of the subject, I shall turn to the passages I most particularly object to in the works of the authors just mentioned; but I must first point out that my objection covers the whole drift of those books, which tend, in my opinion, to degrade one half of the human species and to make women pleasing at the cost of every solid virtue.

Yet, to reason on Rousseau’s own ground: if a man did reach a degree of mental perfection when his body reached maturity, it might then be right, in order to make a man and his wife ONE, for her to rely entirely on his understanding; and the graceful ivy clinging to the oak that supported it would form a whole in which strength and beauty stood out equally. But alas! husbands, like their helpmates, are often no more than overgrown children — indeed, thanks to early debauchery, hardly men even in outward form; and if the blind lead the blind, no one need come down from heaven to tell us the result.

In the present corrupt state of society, many causes combine to enslave women by cramping their understandings and sharpening their senses. One of them, which perhaps does more silent harm than all the rest, is their disregard of order.

Doing everything in an orderly way is a most important rule. Yet women, who generally receive only a disorderly sort of education, seldom keep to it with the exactness of men, who are trained to method from infancy. This careless guesswork — for what other word describes the random efforts of a kind of instinctive common sense that has never been tested by reason? — prevents them from drawing general conclusions from facts, so that they do today what they did yesterday, simply because they did it yesterday.

This contempt for the understanding in early life has more damaging effects than is commonly supposed. For the little knowledge that women of strong minds do acquire is, for various reasons, more haphazard than that of men, and it is gained more from sheer observation of real life than from comparing individual observations with the results of experience generalized by reflection. Since their dependent position and domestic occupations draw them more into company, they learn in snatches; and because learning is, in general, only a secondary concern for them, they do not pursue any single branch of it with the persevering ardour needed to give vigour to the faculties and clarity to the judgment. In the present state of society a little learning is required to keep up the character of a gentleman, and boys are made to submit to a few years of discipline. In the education of women, however, the cultivation of the understanding always gives way to acquiring some physical accomplishment; and even then, weakened by confinement and false notions of modesty, the body is kept from attaining the grace and beauty that slack, half-formed limbs never show. Besides, in youth their faculties are not drawn out by rivalry; and since they have no serious scientific study, whatever natural shrewdness they possess is turned too early upon life and manners. They dwell on effects and variations without tracing them back to causes; and complicated rules for regulating behaviour are a poor substitute for simple principles.

As proof that it is education which gives females this appearance of weakness, we may point to the example of military men, who, like women, are sent out into the world before their minds have been furnished with knowledge or strengthened by principles. The results are similar. Soldiers pick up a little superficial knowledge, snatched from the muddy stream of conversation, and by constantly mixing in company they acquire what is called a knowledge of the world; and this familiarity with manners and customs has often been mistaken for a knowledge of the human heart. But does the raw fruit of casual observation, never tested by a judgment formed through comparing theory with experience, deserve such an honour? Soldiers, like women, practise the minor virtues with meticulous politeness. Where, then, is the difference of sex, when the education has been the same? All the difference I can see arises from the greater advantage of liberty, which lets soldiers see more of life.
It may be a digression from my present subject to make a political remark; but since it arose naturally from the course of my reflections, I shall not pass over it in silence.

Standing armies can never be made up of resolute, robust men. They may be well-drilled machines, but they will seldom include men moved by strong passions or possessed of very vigorous faculties. As for any depth of understanding, I will venture to say that it is as rarely found in the army as among women; and the cause, I maintain, is the same. It may further be noted that officers, too, pay particular attention to their appearance and are fond of dancing, crowded rooms, adventures and ridicule. Like the FAIR sex, they make gallantry the business of their lives. They were taught to please, and they live only to please. Yet they keep their rank in the distinction between the sexes, for they are still thought superior to women — though what that superiority consists in, beyond what I have just described, is hard to discover.
